note: Covers the whole lifecycle of running models on constrained hardware, from model design through runtime optimisation. Relevant to our on-device and edge model sections.
title: A Review on Edge Large Language Models: Design, Execution, and Applications

reading.body:
Running large language models on phones and edge devices requires designing for efficiency at every stage, from initial architecture through runtime execution, and this survey catalogs the full lifecycle of that process.

The paper covers model design, pre-deployment optimization, and runtime inference techniques for constrained hardware. This is a systems problem, not a single breakthrough. Each stage offers different levers for reduction: architectural choices that lower parameters, compression applied before deployment, and inference methods that trade speed or accuracy to fit memory and power budgets. The techniques must work across hardware diversity since edge devices range widely in capability.

For AI scaling, this matters because on-device models consume power and real estate at the user's end rather than at a datacenter. They reduce the compute that must flow through the grid and be housed in buildings. The tradeoff is that edge deployment fragments compute across millions of devices, creating coordination and update challenges that centralized inference does not face.

This survey does not cover the full infrastructure picture: datacenter models still train centrally and often require server resources to prepare edge versions. It also does not compare the total power cost of distributed edge inference against centralized inference at scale. What it does is map the technical design space for making that tradeoff viable at all.

explain_beginner: Large AI language models normally need powerful servers with lots of memory to run, which is why most chatbot apps send your question over the internet to a data center instead of processing it on your phone. This paper reviews the growing body of research on shrinking these models so they can run directly on a phone, watch, or other small device instead. It surveys the main techniques researchers use, compressing a model's internal numbers into simpler formats, trimming out less important parts of the model, and training smaller models to imitate larger ones, along with the specialized phone chips built to run them efficiently. Running AI on device instead of in the cloud means it can work without an internet connection, respond faster since there is no network delay, and keep personal data on the device rather than sending it to a company's servers. The review is a map of current techniques and open problems, not a claim that on device AI already matches full sized cloud models.
explain_business: Companies considering on device AI features, for privacy, offline functionality, or reduced server costs, can use this review as a technical map of which compression techniques and hardware platforms are mature enough to build on today versus which remain research problems. The identified gap between how much compute modern LLMs need and what current mobile and edge chips can provide means realistic on device products right now generally require smaller, purpose built models rather than shrunk versions of frontier scale systems, a distinction that affects both user experience expectations and engineering timelines. The review's point that compact model development is still concentrated among large, well resourced companies is a relevant competitive fact for smaller teams planning to build on open compact models like Phi or Gemma rather than training their own from scratch. This is an active engineering area now, suitable for near term feature planning, not a distant research horizon.
explain_practitioner: This review surveys the full edge LLM deployment pipeline in three stages, model level compression, pre deployment optimization, and runtime inference. It covers quantization approaches from weight only methods like GPTQ and AWQ to combined weight activation methods like SmoothQuant, structured and unstructured pruning techniques such as SparseGPT and LLM-Pruner, and both white box and black box knowledge distillation, alongside compact architectures such as Phi, Gemma, and OpenELM built with efficiency features like grouped query attention. It maps these techniques onto real edge hardware, including Qualcomm Snapdragon and MediaTek Dimensity mobile chips and dedicated NPUs, and onto inference frameworks such as llama.cpp and MLC-LLM. The authors identify a widening gap between the computational demand of LLMs, measured in TFLOPs, and the capacity of edge hardware, measured in TOPS, as the central unresolved constraint, and separately note that catastrophic forgetting during on device continual learning and fragmentation across heterogeneous device hardware remain open engineering problems without standardized solutions.
